problem_motivation.content: Scalable integration of high-quality crystalline GaP thin films on insulating substrates is still difficult.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, scalable integration of high-quality crystalline GaP thin films with insulating substrates remains a significant challenge [16].

problem_motivation.content: Applying CIS to GaP photonic integration has seen little exploration compared with other semiconductors.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Although CIS is widely established in other semiconductor material systems, its application to GaP photonic integration remains comparatively unexplored [20, 21].

prior_approach.content: Most existing GaP photonic platforms use epitaxially grown GaP/AlGaP heterostructures made by MBE or MOCVD with sacrificial-layer removal and thin-film transfer.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Most of the demonstrated GaP photonic platforms rely on epitaxially grown GaP/AlGaP heterostructures fabricated by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) [4, 17] or metal–organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) [18], followed by selective sacrificial-layer removal and thin film transfer processes.

prior_approach.content: Direct wafer bonding with oxide intermediate layers has been used to integrate GaP thin films on insulating substrates.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Direct wafer bonding has emerged as an attractive route for integrating GaP thin films with insulating substrates, particularly in combination with oxide intermediate layers [4].

prior_limitation.content: These epitaxial-stack approaches are tied to predefined stacks and substrate-specific growth, restricting substrate choice and heterogeneous integration.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: While these approaches have enabled high-performance photonic devices, they intrinsically depend on predefined epitaxial thin film stacks and substrate-specific layer growth architectures, limiting substrate choice and heterogeneous integration strategies [16].

prior_limitation.content: Previously demonstrated bonded GaP photonic platforms still depend mainly on epitaxially grown thin films from sacrificial-layer transfer.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Nevertheless, previously demonstrated bonded GaP photonic platforms still primarily rely on epitaxially grown thin film structures derived from sacrificial-layer transfer processes [19].

prior_limitation.content: Because implantation conditions and substrates both changed, the continuity improvement cannot be uniquely assigned to co-implantation.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Because the two experiments differed in both implantation conditions and target substrate, the improved continuity of the H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted sample cannot be attributed uniquely to the co-implantation process.

rejected_alternative.content: The work positions itself against GaP thin-film platforms based on heteroepitaxial growth or sacrificial-layer release, favoring a substrate-independent integration approach.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Unlike GaP thin-film platforms that rely on heteroepitaxial growth or sacrificial-layer release, the presented approach enables the flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films, independent of both donor and target substrates.

rejected_alternative.content: Rather than relying on epitaxially grown sacrificial-layer-derived thin films, the paper contrasts its use of CIS, which decouples the active film from the growth substrate.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: In contrast, crystal ion slicing (CIS) enables flexible transfer of crystalline thin films by decoupling the active GaP thin film from the original growth substrate.

rejected_alternative.content: The approach is positioned as an alternative to epitaxial-growth/sacrificial-layer-release platforms.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: providing a flexible alternative to conventional platforms based on epitaxial growth and sacrificial-layer release

causal_claim.content: Post-transfer annealing causes the films to attain near-bulk crystalline quality, low residual strain, smooth surfaces, and homogeneous bonding interfaces.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Following post-transfer annealing, the films exhibit near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain, smooth surfaces suitable for nanophotonic fabrication, and homogeneous bonding interfaces.

causal_claim.content: Annealing restores the linear optical dispersion toward that of epitaxially grown GaP and yields low estimated absorption loss.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Furthermore, annealing restores the linear optical dispersion (n and k) approaching that of epitaxially grown GaP with estimated plane wave absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

causal_claim.content: Film transfer followed by annealing substantially reduces implantation-induced crystal damage and restores near-bulk crystal quality with low residual strain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Following GaP film transfer and annealing, implantation-induced crystal damage is substantially reduced, restoring the films toward near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain.

causal_claim.content: Ion implantation creates a buried damage layer that enables controlled exfoliation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: These samples were subjected to ion implantation of helium (He⁺) and co-implantation of hydrogen/helium (H⁺/He⁺) species, respectively to create a buried damage layer that enables controlled exfoliation.

causal_claim.content: The SiO2 interlayer facilitates bonding and provides adhesion/mechanical support.
causal_claim.evidence_span: a 700 nm silicon dioxide (SiO₂) interlayer is deposited onto the GaP surface (2) to facilitate subsequent bonding and to act as an adhesion and mechanical support layer.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing induces blistering and crack propagation, causing exfoliation and transfer of the GaP film.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Subsequent to the bonding, controlled thermal annealing in a conventional furnace in air, induces hydrogen- and helium-related blistering and crack propagation along the weakened buried layer, resulting in exfoliation and transfer of the GaP thin film onto the target substrate after approximately 3 h at 350 °C

causal_claim.content: Higher-temperature annealing reconstructs the lattice, reduces implantation defects, and restores crystallinity.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Following thin film transfer, the sample undergoes a higher-temperature annealing at 600 °C in vacuum (4), which serves to reconstruct the GaP lattice, reduce implantation-induced point defects and dislocation complexes, and restore crystallinity toward bulk-like structural quality.

causal_claim.content: The implantation depth distribution matches the target thickness and ensures proper cleaving-plane damage deposition.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This depth distribution closely matches the targeted thin film thickness and ensures optimal energy deposition and defect accumulation within the intended cleaving plane.

causal_claim.content: A lower Qz reflects expansion of the out-of-plane lattice parameter, likely from implanted ions.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This decrease in Qz/(2π) clearly reflects an expansion of the out-of-plane lattice parameter, likely due to the presence of implanted ions.

causal_claim.content: Increased peak widths indicate an implantation-induced strain gradient and reduced long-range order.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The peak widths increase to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.84×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 8.42×10⁻³ nm⁻¹, demonstrating a significant implantation-induced strain gradient accompanied by reduced long-range order.

causal_claim.content: Enhanced diffuse scattering confirms implantation-induced defects from slicing and bonding.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The enhanced diffuse scattering further confirms the presence of implantation-induced defects introduced during the crystal ion slicing and bonding processes.

causal_claim.content: Annealing largely relieves implantation-induced lattice strain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C in vacuum for 12 h (Fig. 3c), the diffraction peak shifts back towards the pristine bulk GaP reciprocal lattice position... indicating that the implantation-induced lattice strain has been largely relieved.

causal_claim.content: The increased LO linewidth is consistent with structural damage and more phonon scattering.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the LO linewidth increases to 12.13 ± 0.88 cm⁻¹, consistent with substantial structural damage and increased phonon scattering.

causal_claim.content: The lower LO linewidth after annealing shows recovery of crystalline order and reduced local strain fluctuations.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The LO linewidth decreases to 3.97 ± 0.46 cm⁻¹, demonstrating substantial recovery of crystalline order and a reduction in local strain fluctuations.

causal_claim.content: Reappearance of the TO phonon indicates recovery of lattice vibrations obscured before annealing.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The TO phonon is again clearly resolved at 357.12 ± 1.14 cm⁻¹ with a linewidth of 8.31 ± 3.14 cm⁻¹, indicating recovery of the lattice vibrations that were obscured in the as-transferred film.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing reduces implantation defects, restores phonon modes, and improves structural quality.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Overall, the Raman results provide quantitative evidence that thermal annealing effectively reduces implantation-induced defects, restores well-defined optical phonon modes, and significantly improves the structural quality of the transferred GaP film.

causal_claim.content: The unannealed transferred film has lower n and higher k due to implantation defects, strain inhomogeneity, and reduced lattice order.
causal_claim.evidence_span: These differences are attributed to implantation-induced defects, strain inhomogeneity, and reduced lattice order, which modify the dielectric response and introduce sub-bandgap optical absorption.

causal_claim.content: Annealing shifts the refractive index toward bulk GaP and greatly lowers extinction coefficient.
causal_claim.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 12 h, the refractive-index n of the thin film shifts toward that of bulk GaP and becomes nearly identical to the pristine bulk GaP at longer wavelengths. More importantly, the extinction coefficient decreases by approximately one to two orders of magnitude relative to the unannealed film throughout much of the near infrared spectral range.

causal_claim.content: Reduced k indicates removal or passivation of optically active implantation defects and lower sub-bandgap loss.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This strong reduction in k demonstrates the removal or passivation of optically active implantation defects and a corresponding decrease in sub-bandgap optical loss.

causal_claim.content: Ellipsometry shows substantial optical recovery after annealing, consistent with strain relaxation, defect reduction, and improved crystalline order.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Overall, the ellipsometry results demonstrate substantial optical recovery after annealing and are consistent with the RSM and Raman measurements, which independently reveal strain relaxation, defect reduction, and improved crystalline order in the transferred GaP film.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing substantially restores GaP structural and optical properties after implantation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thermal annealing substantially restores the structural and optical properties of GaP after ion implantation.

causal_claim.content: Compatibility with SOI is attractive for silicon photonics and CMOS processing while avoiding epitaxial GaP growth.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Its compatibility with silicon-on-insulator substrates is particularly attractive for silicon photonics and CMOS processing, while avoiding epitaxial GaP growth.

causal_claim.content: GaP's large bandgap and high refractive index make the platform promising for visible-wavelength applications.
causal_claim.evidence_span: GaP’s large bandgap and high refractive index also make the platform promising for visible-wavelength applications, enabling increased integration density and access to a broad range of light sources, quantum emitters, and high-quality electro-optic devices.

causal_claim.content: Ion slicing and bonding introduced lattice strain and structural disorder.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Overall, the reciprocal space maps demonstrate that the ion slicing and bonding processes introduce lattice strain and structural disorder

causal_claim.content: Post-bonding annealing relaxed implantation-induced strain and brought the film closer to bulk crystal structure.
causal_claim.evidence_span: whereas post-bonding annealing effectively relaxes much of the implantation-induced strain, bringing the transferred GaP thin film closer to the structural state of the bulk crystal.

causal_claim.content: Annealing relieved implantation-induced damage and local strain fluctuations, restoring crystalline quality.
causal_claim.evidence_span: whereas post-bonding annealing effectively relieves implantation-induced damage, reduces local strain fluctuations, and restores the crystalline quality of the transferred GaP film.

mechanism_principle.content: Possible causes of the localized transfer defects include roughness, contamination, bonding variations, or crack-propagation variations.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The localized nature of these defects could arise from several factors, including surface roughness, particulate contamination, local variations in interfacial bonding, or spatial variations in crack initiation and propagation during thermal exfoliation.

mechanism_principle.content: The isolated interface defect may stem from dust or a local surface imperfection.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This defect may, for example, have originated from a dust particle or another localized surface imperfection.

mechanism_principle.content: Other factors such as substrate properties, preparation, contamination, and bonding could also affect transfer morphology.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Substrate-dependent surface properties, surface preparation, local contamination, and differences in interfacial bonding may also have contributed to the observed transfer morphologies.

mechanism_principle.content: Hydrogen forms H2-containing platelets and helium stabilizes/pressurizes defect clusters, together helping create a buried fracture plane.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: During thermal annealing, implanted hydrogen can promote the formation and growth of H₂-containing platelets, while helium can interact with implantation-induced vacancies and contribute to the stabilization and pressurization of subsurface defect clusters. Their combined action may facilitate the formation of a buried fracture plane and promote layer separation.

mechanism_principle.content: Elongation along Qz indicates a wider distribution of the out-of-plane lattice parameter.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The peak is elongated predominantly along the Qz/(2π) direction, indicating an increased distribution of the out-of-plane lattice parameter.

mechanism_principle.content: The still-broader annealed peak likely indicates remaining strain gradients.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: although it is noticeably broader (FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 1.14×10⁻² nm⁻¹, FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 1.30×10⁻² nm⁻¹) than that of the pristine bulk GaP and the film before annealing likely indicating remaining strain gradients.

mechanism_principle.content: The broadened Raman background indicates lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: indicative of implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.

mechanism_principle.content: Irregularities near 500–600 nm likely arise because ellipsometry is more sensitive near the absorption edge to thickness, roughness, and interface assumptions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The spectral irregularities observed around 500–600 nm occur close to the GaP absorption edge, where the optical constants are strongly dispersive and the ellipsometry fitting is more sensitive to the assumed film thickness, surface roughness, and interface model.

mechanism_principle.content: Out-of-plane elongated scattering indicates a distribution of lattice spacings from implantation-induced strain and structural disorder.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The scattering is elongated primarily along the out-of-plane direction, indicating an increased distribution of lattice spacings associated with implantation-induced strain and structural disorder.

mechanism_principle.content: The reduced Qz indicates out-of-plane lattice expansion likely caused by implanted ions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The significant reduction in Qz/(2π) indicates an expansion of the out-of-plane lattice parameter compared with pristine bulk GaP likely due to the presence of implanted ions

mechanism_principle.content: Elevated Raman background and broadened phonons are attributed to implantation-induced disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the Raman spectrum exhibits a substantially elevated background together with broadened phonon features, reflecting implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.

hypothesis_statement.content: The proposed approach should enable flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films regardless of donor and target substrate choice.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: the presented approach enables the flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films, independent of both donor and target substrates.

hypothesis_statement.content: The demonstrated method is proposed as a scalable route to high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with heterogeneous integration and BEOL CMOS processing.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The demonstrated approach establishes a scalable pathway toward high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with versatile heterogeneous integration and back-end-of-line CMOS processing.

hypothesis_statement.content: The work proposes that CIS plus plasma-activated direct wafer bonding can fabricate high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here, we demonstrate the fabrication of high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films using CIS and plasma-activated direct wafer bonding onto silica and SiO₂/Si substrates.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach is presented as a scalable route to low-loss, high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with heterogeneous integration and BEOL CMOS processing.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This approach establishes a scalable pathway toward low-loss, high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with versatile heterogeneous integration and back-end-of-line CMOS processing.

hypothesis_statement.content: H+/He+ co-implantation plausibly facilitates controlled layer separation.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Nevertheless, H⁺/He⁺ co-implantation provides a physically plausible mechanism for facilitating controlled layer separation.

hypothesis_statement.content: The work demonstrates CIS plus direct bonding as an approach for high-quality GaP-on-insulator films.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: We have demonstrated an approach to fabricating high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films by combining crystal ion slicing (CIS) with direct wafer bonding.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach may enable next-generation active and quantum photonic integrated circuits.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This approach may therefore pave the way toward next-generation active and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the transferred films show near-bulk crystal quality, low strain, smooth surfaces, and homogeneous interfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following post-transfer annealing, the films exhibit near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain, smooth surfaces suitable for nanophotonic fabrication, and homogeneous bonding interfaces.

evidence_result.content: The annealed films have optical dispersion approaching epitaxial GaP and an estimated absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Furthermore, annealing restores the linear optical dispersion (n and k) approaching that of epitaxially grown GaP with estimated plane wave absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: The transferred films show uniform, low-defect bonding interfaces and smooth ion-sliced surfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The transferred films exhibit uniform, defect-minimized bonding interfaces and smooth ion-sliced surfaces.

evidence_result.content: The refractive indices are close to bulk GaP across visible and near-IR, with estimated absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Their refractive indices closely match those of bulk GaP across the visible and near-infrared spectral ranges, with an estimated planar-wave absorption loss of only 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: Simulations place implanted He and H near the target film thickness with about 200 nm spread.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Asymmetric Gaussian fits indicate a projected ion range (Rₚ) centered at 844.5 nm and 806.5 nm beneath the GaP surface for He and H ions respectively, with a longitudinal straggle of ~200 nm full width at half maximum (FWHM).

evidence_result.content: The He+-implanted sample shows no extended interfacial voids in IR imaging.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the IR transmission image of the He⁺-implanted sample shows no extended interfacial voids within the bonded area

evidence_result.content: The He+-implanted sample has a discontinuous, porous transferred GaP layer.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The corresponding OM image, however, reveals a discontinuous GaP layer containing numerous circular regions in which material was not transferred, resulting in a porous appearance.

evidence_result.content: The H+/He+ co-implanted sample has an almost void-free bonded interface except for one isolated defect.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted sample shown in Fig. 2b also exhibits an almost void-free bonded interface in the IR transmission image, apart from a single isolated defect marked by the yellow arrow.

evidence_result.content: The H+/He+ co-implanted sample shows a largely continuous and homogeneous GaP layer.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the corresponding OM image shows a largely continuous and homogeneous GaP layer across the target substrate.

evidence_result.content: Both implantation/bonding configurations achieved layer transfer, but with very different film continuity.
evidence_result.evidence_span: These observations demonstrate that GaP layer transfer was achieved using both implantation and bonding configurations, although the resulting films exhibited substantially different degrees of continuity.

evidence_result.content: The co-implanted film's higher continuity is consistent with the proposed co-implantation mechanism.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The comparatively high continuity of the co-implanted film observed here is consistent with this mechanism

evidence_result.content: The results establish proof of concept for GaP thin-film transfer using both He+ and H+/He+ implantation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Taken together, the results establish proof of concept for GaP thin-film transfer using both He⁺ implantation and H⁺/He⁺ co-implantation under the respective processing conditions.

evidence_result.content: Among tested specimens, the H+/He+ film on fused silica had better continuity and was chosen for further study.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Among the specimens investigated, the H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted GaP layer transferred to fused silica exhibited the greater film continuity and was therefore selected for the subsequent analyses.

evidence_result.content: SEM shows continuous interfaces without resolvable voids in the inspected cross section.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Within the inspected cross section, the interfaces between the GaP film and the bonding SiO₂ layer, as well as between the SiO₂ layer and the fused silica substrate, appear continuous and free of resolvable voids.

evidence_result.content: The transferred GaP film thickness is about 790 nm, matching the simulated ion ranges.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The measured GaP film thickness is approximately 790 nm, in good agreement with the projected ion ranges of H⁺ and He⁺ obtained from the simulations shown in Fig. 1b.

evidence_result.content: AFM finds an RMS roughness of about 4.9 nm on the transferred surface.
evidence_result.evidence_span: An RMS roughness of approximately 4.9 nm was obtained

evidence_result.content: The annealed film appears macroscopically homogeneous and transmissive, consistent with prior imaging.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The relatively homogeneous macroscopic appearance and optical transmission across most of the film are consistent with the IR transmission and OM observations in Fig. 2b.

evidence_result.content: After slicing and bonding, the diffraction peak broadens and diffuse scattering increases.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and direct bonding to silica (Fig. 3b), the diffraction peak becomes noticeably broader and is accompanied by pronounced diffuse scattering extending around the Bragg reflection.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the diffraction peak is more symmetric and centered near the nominal GaP lattice position.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The diffraction peak appears more symmetric and centered on the nominal GaP reciprocal lattice position

evidence_result.content: After slicing and bonding, the LO phonon remains visible but the Raman spectrum broadens with elevated background.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and bonding, the LO phonon remains clearly visible, confirming preservation of the crystalline GaP phase, but the Raman spectrum becomes significantly broadened and is superimposed on an elevated background

evidence_result.content: After annealing, Raman background is reduced and phonon features sharpen significantly.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 12 h, the Raman spectrum exhibits a marked reduction in the disorder-related background together with significantly sharper phonon features.

evidence_result.content: The He+/H+ co-implanted film has greater initial lattice expansion and disorder than the He+-only film.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the He⁺/H⁺ co-implanted film exhibits greater initial out-of-plane lattice expansion and stronger implantation-induced disorder, as indicated by its larger negative ΔQz and broader LO Raman linewidth before annealing.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, both films recover close to the pristine bulk lattice position.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following annealing, both films recover closely to the pristine bulk GaP lattice position.

evidence_result.content: The measured pristine bulk GaP shows anomalously large long-wavelength extinction, implying poorer optical quality than expected.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine bulk GaP sample measured here exhibits an anomalously large extinction coefficient at long wavelengths, suggesting appreciable defect-related absorption and lower optical quality than expected for high-quality bulk GaP.

evidence_result.content: The annealed ion-sliced film has bulk-like n dispersion and the lowest near-IR k among compared samples.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the annealed ion-sliced GaP film combines bulk-like refractive-index dispersion with the lowest near-infrared extinction coefficient among the samples considered.

evidence_result.content: Assuming full confinement, the annealed film's material-absorption upper-bound loss reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Assuming complete optical confinement within the film, it represents an upper bound on the material-absorption contribution to the waveguide loss and reaches 0.9 dB/cm at the telecommunication wavelength of 1550 nm.

evidence_result.content: The transferred films have smooth surfaces and homogeneous, defect-minimized bonding interfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The transferred films exhibit smooth surfaces and homogeneous, defect-minimized bonding interfaces suitable for subsequent nanophotonic processing.

evidence_result.content: Raman, XRD, and RSM show recovered phonon modes, improved crystalline order, and reduced lattice strain after annealing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Raman spectroscopy reveals the recovery of well-defined optical phonon modes, while X-ray diffraction and reciprocal-space mapping show improved crystalline order and reduced implantation-induced lattice strain.

evidence_result.content: The refractive index and extinction coefficient approach those of crystalline GaP after annealing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Consistently, the refractive index and extinction coefficient approaches those of crystalline GaP.

evidence_result.content: The calculated propagation loss reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The wavelength-dependent plane-wave propagation loss, calculated from the extinction coefficient of the annealed film, reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: Pristine bulk GaP showed a sharp diffraction peak with minimal diffuse scattering and narrow widths, indicating high crystal quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine bulk GaP crystal (Fig. 3a) exhibits a sharp, diffraction peak with minimal diffuse scattering, characteristic of a high-quality single crystal. The narrow-fitted widths of FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 1.63×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 5.05×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ confirm the excellent crystalline quality and low defect density of the pristine bulk material.

evidence_result.content: After ion slicing and bonding, the diffraction peak broadened, diffuse scattering increased, and the fitted peak shifted, showing degraded lattice quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and direct bonding to silica (Fig. S1b), the diffraction peak becomes noticeably broader and is accompanied by pronounced diffuse scattering surrounding the Bragg reflection. The fitted peak shifts to (Qx, Qz)/(2π) = (5.1912, 7.3321) nm⁻¹.

evidence_result.content: Peak widths increased after ion slicing and bonding, demonstrating strain broadening and increased lattice disorder.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The fitted peak widths increase to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.49 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 8.11 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹, demonstrating substantial implantation-induced strain broadening and increased lattice disorder introduced during the ion slicing and bonding processes.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the diffraction peak moved closer to bulk position and became more localized, indicating recovery.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 7 h in vacuum (Fig. S1c), the diffraction peak moves back closer to the nominal bulk GaP reciprocal lattice position, with the fitted peak located at (Qx, Qz)/(2π) = (5.1910, 7.3362) nm⁻¹ indicating a significant recovery of the implantation-induced lattice distortion, particularly in the out-of-plane direction. Compared with the unannealed film, the diffuse scattering halo changes shape and the Bragg reflection appears more localized.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, peak widths decreased to values close to pristine bulk, showing improved crystal quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The fitted peak widths decrease to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.73 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 6.88 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹. These values are close to the pristine bulk GaP, showing that thermal annealing substantially relieves strain and improves the crystalline quality of the transferred GaP layer.

evidence_result.content: Pristine GaP Raman showed sharp TO and LO phonon modes characteristic of excellent crystalline quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine GaP spectrum exhibits the characteristic transverse optical (TO) and longitudinal optical (LO) phonon modes of crystalline GaP, with sharp and well-defined Raman peaks indicative of excellent crystalline quality.

evidence_result.content: The unannealed film showed elevated Raman background and broadened phonons, with shifted and broadened TO and broader LO linewidth.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following He+ crystal ion slicing and direct bonding (unannealed film), the Raman spectrum exhibits a substantially elevated background together with broadened phonon features, reflecting implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering. Although both TO and LO modes remain observable, the TO peak shifts to 354.58 ± 2.69 cm⁻¹ and broadens to 9.11 ± 7.38 cm⁻¹, while the LO linewidth increases to 8.84 ± 0.84 cm⁻¹.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, Raman background was reduced and phonon modes sharpened, with TO and LO linewidths decreasing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 7 h, the Raman spectrum shows a marked recovery of crystalline quality. The background scattering is substantially reduced, and both phonon modes become sharper and more prominent. The TO phonon shifts to 358.29 ± 0.72 cm⁻¹ with a reduced linewidth of 6.46 ± 1.98 cm⁻¹, while the LO phonon linewidth decreases dramatically to 3.88 ± 0.38 cm⁻¹, becoming even narrower than that of the pristine bulk crystal.

constraint.content: Direct bonding requires sub-nanometer surface roughness and high surface energy.
constraint.evidence_span: to achieve the sub-nanometer surface roughness and high surface energy required for direct wafer bonding

constraint.content: Current data cannot distinguish the relative contributions of the possible defect mechanisms.
constraint.evidence_span: The available data does not allow the relative contributions of these possible mechanisms to be distinguished.

constraint.content: A systematic repeated comparison on identical substrates is needed to isolate implantation effects conclusively.
constraint.evidence_span: A systematic comparison involving repeated experiments on identical target substrates would be required to separate these effects and establish the influence of the implantation conditions conclusively.

constraint.content: The present results do not prove co-implantation was the sole or dominant cause of the continuity difference.
constraint.evidence_span: although the present results do not demonstrate that co-implantation was the sole or dominant cause of the difference between the two samples.

constraint.content: Choosing the fused-silica H+/He+ specimen is not a general comparison of implantation schemes or substrates.
constraint.evidence_span: This selection is based on the quality of the obtained specimen and should not be interpreted as a general comparison of the two implantation schemes or target substrates.

constraint.content: Small k values are sensitive to measurement uncertainty and model assumptions, so artifacts cannot be ruled out.
constraint.evidence_span: because small k values are particularly sensitive to measurement uncertainty and ellipsometric model assumptions, contributions from fitting artifacts, surface roughness, or backside reflections cannot be excluded.

constraint.content: The measured bulk sample should not be treated as representing intrinsic high-quality bulk GaP absorption.
constraint.evidence_span: The measured sample should therefore not be regarded as representative of the intrinsic absorption limit of high-quality bulk GaP.

constraint.content: That loss is only an upper bound if complete optical confinement in the GaP film is assumed.
constraint.evidence_span: Assuming complete optical confinement within the GaP film, this value represents an upper bound on the material-absorption contribution to the waveguide loss.

problem_motivation.content: Scalable integration of high-quality crystalline GaP thin films on insulating substrates remains a significant challenge, and the application of crystal ion slicing (CIS) to GaP photonic integration has remained comparatively unexplored relative to other semiconductor systems.
evidence_spans: However, scalable integration of high-quality crystalline GaP thin films with insulating substrates remains a significant challenge [16].
Although CIS is widely established in other semiconductor material systems, its application to GaP photonic integration remains comparatively unexplored [20, 21].

prior_approach.content: Prior GaP photonic platforms typically used epitaxially grown GaP/AlGaP heterostructures fabricated by MBE or MOCVD, followed by selective sacrificial-layer removal and thin-film transfer; direct wafer bonding, particularly with oxide intermediate layers, was also used to integrate GaP thin films on insulating substrates.
evidence_spans: Most of the demonstrated GaP photonic platforms rely on epitaxially grown GaP/AlGaP heterostructures fabricated by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) [4, 17] or metal–organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) [18], followed by selective sacrificial-layer removal and thin film transfer processes.
Direct wafer bonding has emerged as an attractive route for integrating GaP thin films with insulating substrates, particularly in combination with oxide intermediate layers [4].

prior_limitation.content: Prior GaP photonic platform approaches depend on predefined epitaxial/grown thin-film stacks and substrate-specific growth or sacrificial-layer transfer, which restricts substrate choice, heterogeneous integration, and flexibility of bonded platforms.
evidence_spans: While these approaches have enabled high-performance photonic devices, they intrinsically depend on predefined epitaxial thin film stacks and substrate-specific layer growth architectures, limiting substrate choice and heterogeneous integration strategies [16].
Nevertheless, previously demonstrated bonded GaP photonic platforms still primarily rely on epitaxially grown thin film structures derived from sacrificial-layer transfer processes [19].

prior_limitation.content: In prior implantation experiments, because both implantation conditions and the target substrate changed simultaneously, the observed continuity improvement could not be uniquely attributed to the co-implantation process.
evidence_spans: Because the two experiments differed in both implantation conditions and target substrate, the improved continuity of the H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted sample cannot be attributed uniquely to the co-implantation process.

rejected_alternative.content: Conventional GaP thin-film platforms based on heteroepitaxial/epitaxial growth and sacrificial-layer release are rejected in favor of a crystal ion slicing (CIS)-based, substrate-independent transfer approach that decouples the active GaP film from the original growth substrate.
evidence_spans: Unlike GaP thin-film platforms that rely on heteroepitaxial growth or sacrificial-layer release, the presented approach enables the flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films, independent of both donor and target substrates.
In contrast, crystal ion slicing (CIS) enables flexible transfer of crystalline thin films by decoupling the active GaP thin film from the original growth substrate.
providing a flexible alternative to conventional platforms based on epitaxial growth and sacrificial-layer release

causal_claim.content: Ion implantation creates a buried damage layer at the intended cleaving plane, enabling controlled exfoliation/cleaving of a GaP film with the target thickness.
evidence_spans: These samples were subjected to ion implantation of helium (He⁺) and co-implantation of hydrogen/helium (H⁺/He⁺) species, respectively to create a buried damage layer that enables controlled exfoliation.
This depth distribution closely matches the targeted thin film thickness and ensures optimal energy deposition and defect accumulation within the intended cleaving plane.

causal_claim.content: The SiO2 interlayer facilitates bonding and serves as an adhesion/mechanical support layer.
evidence_spans: a 700 nm silicon dioxide (SiO₂) interlayer is deposited onto the GaP surface (2) to facilitate subsequent bonding and to act as an adhesion and mechanical support layer.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing after bonding induces hydrogen-/helium-related blistering and crack propagation along the weakened buried layer, causing exfoliation and transfer of the GaP film onto the target substrate.
evidence_spans: Subsequent to the bonding, controlled thermal annealing in a conventional furnace in air, induces hydrogen- and helium-related blistering and crack propagation along the weakened buried layer, resulting in exfoliation and transfer of the GaP thin film onto the target substrate after approximately 3 h at 350 °C

causal_claim.content: Ion slicing/implantation and bonding introduce structural damage, including lattice strain, out-of-plane lattice expansion likely from implanted ions, strain gradients, reduced long-range order, enhanced diffuse scattering, and broader LO phonon linewidth due to increased phonon scattering.
evidence_spans: This decrease in Qz/(2π) clearly reflects an expansion of the out-of-plane lattice parameter, likely due to the presence of implanted ions.

The peak widths increase to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.84×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 8.42×10⁻³ nm⁻¹, demonstrating a significant implantation-induced strain gradient accompanied by reduced long-range order.
The enhanced diffuse scattering further confirms the presence of implantation-induced defects introduced during the crystal ion slicing and bonding processes.
the LO linewidth increases to 12.13 ± 0.88 cm⁻¹, consistent with substantial structural damage and increased phonon scattering.
Overall, the reciprocal space maps demonstrate that the ion slicing and bonding processes introduce lattice strain and structural disorder

causal_claim.content: In the unannealed transferred film, implantation-induced defects, strain inhomogeneity, and reduced lattice order cause lower refractive index n and higher extinction coefficient k, introducing sub-bandgap optical absorption.
evidence_spans: These differences are attributed to implantation-induced defects, strain inhomogeneity, and reduced lattice order, which modify the dielectric response and introduce sub-bandgap optical absorption.

causal_claim.content: Higher-temperature/post-transfer annealing reconstructs the GaP lattice, reduces implantation-induced point defects and dislocation complexes, relieves lattice strain and local strain fluctuations, and substantially reduces crystal damage, restoring the film toward near-bulk/bulk-like crystalline quality and structure.
evidence_spans: Following thin film transfer, the sample undergoes a higher-temperature annealing at 600 °C in vacuum (4), which serves to reconstruct the GaP lattice, reduce implantation-induced point defects and dislocation complexes, and restore crystallinity toward bulk-like structural quality.
Following GaP film transfer and annealing, implantation-induced crystal damage is substantially reduced, restoring the films toward near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain.

After annealing at 600 °C in vacuum for 12 h (Fig. 3c), the diffraction peak shifts back towards the pristine bulk GaP reciprocal lattice position... indicating that the implantation-induced lattice strain has been largely relieved.
whereas post-bonding annealing effectively relaxes much of the implantation-induced strain, bringing the transferred GaP thin film closer to the structural state of the bulk crystal.
whereas post-bonding annealing effectively relieves implantation-induced damage, reduces local strain fluctuations, and restores the crystalline quality of the transferred GaP film.
Following post-transfer annealing, the films exhibit near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain, smooth surfaces suitable for nanophotonic fabrication, and homogeneous bonding interfaces.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing restores phonon/lattice vibrational signatures by reducing implantation defects: the LO linewidth narrows, the TO phonon reappears, and overall structural quality improves.
evidence_spans: The LO linewidth decreases to 3.97 ± 0.46 cm⁻¹, demonstrating substantial recovery of crystalline order and a reduction in local strain fluctuations.
The TO phonon is again clearly resolved at 357.12 ± 1.14 cm⁻¹ with a linewidth of 8.31 ± 3.14 cm⁻¹, indicating recovery of the lattice vibrations that were obscured in the as-transferred film.

Overall, the Raman results provide quantitative evidence that thermal annealing effectively reduces implantation-induced defects, restores well-defined optical phonon modes, and significantly improves the structural quality of the transferred GaP film.

causal_claim.content: Annealing restores the linear optical dispersion toward epitaxial/bulk GaP, shifting n toward bulk values and reducing k by about one to two orders of magnitude; this indicates removal or passivation of optically active implantation defects, lower sub-bandgap/plane-wave absorption loss, and overall optical recovery.
evidence_spans: Furthermore, annealing restores the linear optical dispersion (n and k) approaching that of epitaxially grown GaP with estimated plane wave absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

After annealing at 600 °C for 12 h, the refractive-index n of the thin film shifts toward that of bulk GaP and becomes nearly identical to the pristine bulk GaP at longer wavelengths. More importantly, the extinction coefficient decreases by approximately one to two orders of magnitude relative to the unannealed film throughout much of the near infrared spectral range.
This strong reduction in k demonstrates the removal or passivation of optically active implantation defects and a corresponding decrease in sub-bandgap optical loss.

Overall, the ellipsometry results demonstrate substantial optical recovery after annealing and are consistent with the RSM and Raman measurements, which independently reveal strain relaxation, defect reduction, and improved crystalline order in the transferred GaP film.

causal_claim.content: Overall, thermal annealing substantially restores the structural and optical properties of implanted/transferred GaP films.
evidence_spans: Thermal annealing substantially restores the structural and optical properties of GaP after ion implantation.

causal_claim.content: GaP's compatibility with SOI makes the platform attractive for silicon photonics and CMOS processing while avoiding epitaxial GaP growth.
evidence_spans: Its compatibility with silicon-on-insulator substrates is particularly attractive for silicon photonics and CMOS processing, while avoiding epitaxial GaP growth.

causal_claim.content: GaP's large bandgap and high refractive index make the platform promising for visible-wavelength applications, enabling higher integration density and access to diverse light sources, quantum emitters, and electro-optic devices.
evidence_spans: GaP’s large bandgap and high refractive index also make the platform promising for visible-wavelength applications, enabling increased integration density and access to a broad range of light sources, quantum emitters, and high-quality electro-optic devices.

mechanism_principle.content: Possible causes of the localized transfer defects include roughness, contamination, bonding variations, or crack-propagation variations.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The localized nature of these defects could arise from several factors, including surface roughness, particulate contamination, local variations in interfacial bonding, or spatial variations in crack initiation and propagation during thermal exfoliation.

mechanism_principle.content: The isolated interface defect may stem from dust or a local surface imperfection.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This defect may, for example, have originated from a dust particle or another localized surface imperfection.

mechanism_principle.content: Other factors such as substrate properties, preparation, contamination, and bonding could also affect transfer morphology.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Substrate-dependent surface properties, surface preparation, local contamination, and differences in interfacial bonding may also have contributed to the observed transfer morphologies.

mechanism_principle.content: Hydrogen forms H2-containing platelets and helium stabilizes/pressurizes defect clusters, together helping create a buried fracture plane.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: During thermal annealing, implanted hydrogen can promote the formation and growth of H₂-containing platelets, while helium can interact with implantation-induced vacancies and contribute to the stabilization and pressurization of subsurface defect clusters. Their combined action may facilitate the formation of a buried fracture plane and promote layer separation.

mechanism_principle.content: Elongation along Qz indicates a wider distribution of the out-of-plane lattice parameter.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The peak is elongated predominantly along the Qz/(2π) direction, indicating an increased distribution of the out-of-plane lattice parameter.

mechanism_principle.content: The still-broader annealed peak likely indicates remaining strain gradients.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: although it is noticeably broader (FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 1.14×10⁻² nm⁻¹, FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 1.30×10⁻² nm⁻¹) than that of the pristine bulk GaP and the film before annealing likely indicating remaining strain gradients.

mechanism_principle.content: The broadened Raman background indicates lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: indicative of implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.

mechanism_principle.content: Irregularities near 500–600 nm likely arise because ellipsometry is more sensitive near the absorption edge to thickness, roughness, and interface assumptions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The spectral irregularities observed around 500–600 nm occur close to the GaP absorption edge, where the optical constants are strongly dispersive and the ellipsometry fitting is more sensitive to the assumed film thickness, surface roughness, and interface model.

mechanism_principle.content: Out-of-plane elongated scattering indicates a distribution of lattice spacings from implantation-induced strain and structural disorder.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The scattering is elongated primarily along the out-of-plane direction, indicating an increased distribution of lattice spacings associated with implantation-induced strain and structural disorder.

mechanism_principle.content: The reduced Qz indicates out-of-plane lattice expansion likely caused by implanted ions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The significant reduction in Qz/(2π) indicates an expansion of the out-of-plane lattice parameter compared with pristine bulk GaP likely due to the presence of implanted ions

mechanism_principle.content: Elevated Raman background and broadened phonons are attributed to implantation-induced disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the Raman spectrum exhibits a substantially elevated background together with broadened phonon features, reflecting implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering.

hypothesis_statement.content: The proposed approach should enable flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films regardless of donor and target substrate choice.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: the presented approach enables the flexible integration of crystalline GaP thin films, independent of both donor and target substrates.

hypothesis_statement.content: The demonstrated method is proposed as a scalable route to high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with heterogeneous integration and BEOL CMOS processing.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The demonstrated approach establishes a scalable pathway toward high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with versatile heterogeneous integration and back-end-of-line CMOS processing.

hypothesis_statement.content: The work proposes that CIS plus plasma-activated direct wafer bonding can fabricate high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here, we demonstrate the fabrication of high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films using CIS and plasma-activated direct wafer bonding onto silica and SiO₂/Si substrates.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach is presented as a scalable route to low-loss, high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with heterogeneous integration and BEOL CMOS processing.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This approach establishes a scalable pathway toward low-loss, high-quality GaP thin-film photonics compatible with versatile heterogeneous integration and back-end-of-line CMOS processing.

hypothesis_statement.content: H+/He+ co-implantation plausibly facilitates controlled layer separation.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Nevertheless, H⁺/He⁺ co-implantation provides a physically plausible mechanism for facilitating controlled layer separation.

hypothesis_statement.content: The work demonstrates CIS plus direct bonding as an approach for high-quality GaP-on-insulator films.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: We have demonstrated an approach to fabricating high-quality GaP-on-insulator thin films by combining crystal ion slicing (CIS) with direct wafer bonding.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach may enable next-generation active and quantum photonic integrated circuits.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This approach may therefore pave the way toward next-generation active and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the transferred films show near-bulk crystal quality, low strain, smooth surfaces, and homogeneous interfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following post-transfer annealing, the films exhibit near-bulk crystalline quality with low residual strain, smooth surfaces suitable for nanophotonic fabrication, and homogeneous bonding interfaces.

evidence_result.content: The annealed films have optical dispersion approaching epitaxial GaP and an estimated absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Furthermore, annealing restores the linear optical dispersion (n and k) approaching that of epitaxially grown GaP with estimated plane wave absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: The transferred films show uniform, low-defect bonding interfaces and smooth ion-sliced surfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The transferred films exhibit uniform, defect-minimized bonding interfaces and smooth ion-sliced surfaces.

evidence_result.content: The refractive indices are close to bulk GaP across visible and near-IR, with estimated absorption loss of 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Their refractive indices closely match those of bulk GaP across the visible and near-infrared spectral ranges, with an estimated planar-wave absorption loss of only 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: Simulations place implanted He and H near the target film thickness with about 200 nm spread.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Asymmetric Gaussian fits indicate a projected ion range (Rₚ) centered at 844.5 nm and 806.5 nm beneath the GaP surface for He and H ions respectively, with a longitudinal straggle of ~200 nm full width at half maximum (FWHM).

evidence_result.content: The He+-implanted sample shows no extended interfacial voids in IR imaging.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the IR transmission image of the He⁺-implanted sample shows no extended interfacial voids within the bonded area

evidence_result.content: The He+-implanted sample has a discontinuous, porous transferred GaP layer.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The corresponding OM image, however, reveals a discontinuous GaP layer containing numerous circular regions in which material was not transferred, resulting in a porous appearance.

evidence_result.content: The H+/He+ co-implanted sample has an almost void-free bonded interface except for one isolated defect.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted sample shown in Fig. 2b also exhibits an almost void-free bonded interface in the IR transmission image, apart from a single isolated defect marked by the yellow arrow.

evidence_result.content: The H+/He+ co-implanted sample shows a largely continuous and homogeneous GaP layer.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the corresponding OM image shows a largely continuous and homogeneous GaP layer across the target substrate.

evidence_result.content: Both implantation/bonding configurations achieved layer transfer, but with very different film continuity.
evidence_result.evidence_span: These observations demonstrate that GaP layer transfer was achieved using both implantation and bonding configurations, although the resulting films exhibited substantially different degrees of continuity.

evidence_result.content: The co-implanted film's higher continuity is consistent with the proposed co-implantation mechanism.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The comparatively high continuity of the co-implanted film observed here is consistent with this mechanism

evidence_result.content: The results establish proof of concept for GaP thin-film transfer using both He+ and H+/He+ implantation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Taken together, the results establish proof of concept for GaP thin-film transfer using both He⁺ implantation and H⁺/He⁺ co-implantation under the respective processing conditions.

evidence_result.content: Among tested specimens, the H+/He+ film on fused silica had better continuity and was chosen for further study.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Among the specimens investigated, the H⁺/He⁺ co-implanted GaP layer transferred to fused silica exhibited the greater film continuity and was therefore selected for the subsequent analyses.

evidence_result.content: SEM shows continuous interfaces without resolvable voids in the inspected cross section.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Within the inspected cross section, the interfaces between the GaP film and the bonding SiO₂ layer, as well as between the SiO₂ layer and the fused silica substrate, appear continuous and free of resolvable voids.

evidence_result.content: The transferred GaP film thickness is about 790 nm, matching the simulated ion ranges.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The measured GaP film thickness is approximately 790 nm, in good agreement with the projected ion ranges of H⁺ and He⁺ obtained from the simulations shown in Fig. 1b.

evidence_result.content: AFM finds an RMS roughness of about 4.9 nm on the transferred surface.
evidence_result.evidence_span: An RMS roughness of approximately 4.9 nm was obtained

evidence_result.content: The annealed film appears macroscopically homogeneous and transmissive, consistent with prior imaging.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The relatively homogeneous macroscopic appearance and optical transmission across most of the film are consistent with the IR transmission and OM observations in Fig. 2b.

evidence_result.content: After slicing and bonding, the diffraction peak broadens and diffuse scattering increases.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and direct bonding to silica (Fig. 3b), the diffraction peak becomes noticeably broader and is accompanied by pronounced diffuse scattering extending around the Bragg reflection.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the diffraction peak is more symmetric and centered near the nominal GaP lattice position.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The diffraction peak appears more symmetric and centered on the nominal GaP reciprocal lattice position

evidence_result.content: After slicing and bonding, the LO phonon remains visible but the Raman spectrum broadens with elevated background.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and bonding, the LO phonon remains clearly visible, confirming preservation of the crystalline GaP phase, but the Raman spectrum becomes significantly broadened and is superimposed on an elevated background

evidence_result.content: After annealing, Raman background is reduced and phonon features sharpen significantly.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 12 h, the Raman spectrum exhibits a marked reduction in the disorder-related background together with significantly sharper phonon features.

evidence_result.content: The He+/H+ co-implanted film has greater initial lattice expansion and disorder than the He+-only film.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the He⁺/H⁺ co-implanted film exhibits greater initial out-of-plane lattice expansion and stronger implantation-induced disorder, as indicated by its larger negative ΔQz and broader LO Raman linewidth before annealing.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, both films recover close to the pristine bulk lattice position.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following annealing, both films recover closely to the pristine bulk GaP lattice position.

evidence_result.content: The measured pristine bulk GaP shows anomalously large long-wavelength extinction, implying poorer optical quality than expected.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine bulk GaP sample measured here exhibits an anomalously large extinction coefficient at long wavelengths, suggesting appreciable defect-related absorption and lower optical quality than expected for high-quality bulk GaP.

evidence_result.content: The annealed ion-sliced film has bulk-like n dispersion and the lowest near-IR k among compared samples.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the annealed ion-sliced GaP film combines bulk-like refractive-index dispersion with the lowest near-infrared extinction coefficient among the samples considered.

evidence_result.content: Assuming full confinement, the annealed film's material-absorption upper-bound loss reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Assuming complete optical confinement within the film, it represents an upper bound on the material-absorption contribution to the waveguide loss and reaches 0.9 dB/cm at the telecommunication wavelength of 1550 nm.

evidence_result.content: The transferred films have smooth surfaces and homogeneous, defect-minimized bonding interfaces.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The transferred films exhibit smooth surfaces and homogeneous, defect-minimized bonding interfaces suitable for subsequent nanophotonic processing.

evidence_result.content: Raman, XRD, and RSM show recovered phonon modes, improved crystalline order, and reduced lattice strain after annealing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Raman spectroscopy reveals the recovery of well-defined optical phonon modes, while X-ray diffraction and reciprocal-space mapping show improved crystalline order and reduced implantation-induced lattice strain.

evidence_result.content: The refractive index and extinction coefficient approach those of crystalline GaP after annealing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Consistently, the refractive index and extinction coefficient approaches those of crystalline GaP.

evidence_result.content: The calculated propagation loss reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The wavelength-dependent plane-wave propagation loss, calculated from the extinction coefficient of the annealed film, reaches 0.9 dB/cm at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band.

evidence_result.content: Pristine bulk GaP showed a sharp diffraction peak with minimal diffuse scattering and narrow widths, indicating high crystal quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine bulk GaP crystal (Fig. 3a) exhibits a sharp, diffraction peak with minimal diffuse scattering, characteristic of a high-quality single crystal. The narrow-fitted widths of FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 1.63×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 5.05×10⁻³ nm⁻¹ confirm the excellent crystalline quality and low defect density of the pristine bulk material.

evidence_result.content: After ion slicing and bonding, the diffraction peak broadened, diffuse scattering increased, and the fitted peak shifted, showing degraded lattice quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following crystal ion slicing and direct bonding to silica (Fig. S1b), the diffraction peak becomes noticeably broader and is accompanied by pronounced diffuse scattering surrounding the Bragg reflection. The fitted peak shifts to (Qx, Qz)/(2π) = (5.1912, 7.3321) nm⁻¹.

evidence_result.content: Peak widths increased after ion slicing and bonding, demonstrating strain broadening and increased lattice disorder.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The fitted peak widths increase to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.49 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 8.11 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹, demonstrating substantial implantation-induced strain broadening and increased lattice disorder introduced during the ion slicing and bonding processes.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, the diffraction peak moved closer to bulk position and became more localized, indicating recovery.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 7 h in vacuum (Fig. S1c), the diffraction peak moves back closer to the nominal bulk GaP reciprocal lattice position, with the fitted peak located at (Qx, Qz)/(2π) = (5.1910, 7.3362) nm⁻¹ indicating a significant recovery of the implantation-induced lattice distortion, particularly in the out-of-plane direction. Compared with the unannealed film, the diffuse scattering halo changes shape and the Bragg reflection appears more localized.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, peak widths decreased to values close to pristine bulk, showing improved crystal quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The fitted peak widths decrease to FWHM(Qx)/(2π) = 2.73 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹ and FWHM(Qz)/(2π) = 6.88 × 10⁻³ nm⁻¹. These values are close to the pristine bulk GaP, showing that thermal annealing substantially relieves strain and improves the crystalline quality of the transferred GaP layer.

evidence_result.content: Pristine GaP Raman showed sharp TO and LO phonon modes characteristic of excellent crystalline quality.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pristine GaP spectrum exhibits the characteristic transverse optical (TO) and longitudinal optical (LO) phonon modes of crystalline GaP, with sharp and well-defined Raman peaks indicative of excellent crystalline quality.

evidence_result.content: The unannealed film showed elevated Raman background and broadened phonons, with shifted and broadened TO and broader LO linewidth.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Following He+ crystal ion slicing and direct bonding (unannealed film), the Raman spectrum exhibits a substantially elevated background together with broadened phonon features, reflecting implantation-induced lattice disorder, strain inhomogeneity, and defect-assisted scattering. Although both TO and LO modes remain observable, the TO peak shifts to 354.58 ± 2.69 cm⁻¹ and broadens to 9.11 ± 7.38 cm⁻¹, while the LO linewidth increases to 8.84 ± 0.84 cm⁻¹.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, Raman background was reduced and phonon modes sharpened, with TO and LO linewidths decreasing.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After annealing at 600 °C for 7 h, the Raman spectrum shows a marked recovery of crystalline quality. The background scattering is substantially reduced, and both phonon modes become sharper and more prominent. The TO phonon shifts to 358.29 ± 0.72 cm⁻¹ with a reduced linewidth of 6.46 ± 1.98 cm⁻¹, while the LO phonon linewidth decreases dramatically to 3.88 ± 0.38 cm⁻¹, becoming even narrower than that of the pristine bulk crystal.
